extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing admissible evidence, burdens of proof, and judicial construction in patent infringement litigation — including what a patent proves prima facie, how prior judgments and the state of the art are used, estoppel effects, and who bears which burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent, regular on its face, is prima facie evidence of all the facts essential to its own validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies that the patent, until contradicted, proves the invention resulted from an inventive act; that the patentee or assignor was first and true inventor; that the subject-matter is patentable, new, and useful; not abandoned; lawfully issued to the proper patentee; if a re-issue, that it corresponds with the original; if an extension, that legal requirements were obeyed; that the invention described differs essentially from prior patents; that the specification is without fraud and ambiguity; that the claims are not excessive and clearly define the actual invention; and that the patent has not been surrendered or repealed. This prima facie proof can be overcome only by clear evidence removing all reasonable doubt. The weight of the presumption is increased by re-issue, success in interference proceedings, extension, and long/continuous public recognition (long admitted validity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence of patentee's title and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is prima facie evidence of the patentee's legal title to the patented invention and of his right to maintain an action for infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production of a patent or certified copy makes out a prima facie case as to patentability, validity, and (if plaintiff is patentee) ownership; authenticated instruments of assignment or grant (or copies) satisfy the burden as to title. A patent affords prima facie right to recover from infringers, but does not by itself prove infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent does not prove infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent, though prima facie evidence of validity and title, is not prima facie evidence that the defendant has been guilty of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement remains a separate issue for proof. Where the patent is in evidence and the plaintiff shows infringement, the burden shifts to the defendant to show invalidity or other defenses; the patent itself does not establish the defendant's liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Records of former judgments admissible and their weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Records of former judgments are admissible both as estoppel and for purposes connected to patent interpretation, patentability, and identity of the defendant's device with the patented one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judgment between same parties on same issues by same or superior tribunal is conclusive as to those points and binding on privies. Judgments in co-ordinate or inferior tribunals have weight according to the issues decided and nature of tribunal. Such judgments will generally be followed where there is no new evidence. Judgments are only controlling as to the exact points decided; a former judgment sustaining a patent may be of no weight if present objections raise new questions. Patent Office decisions are prima facie but not conclusive. A judgment is not a precedent unless rendered after full argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When pleadings are closed on the general issue, the burden of proof is on the plaintiff for all averments in his declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove patentability of the invention, validity of the patent, his legal title, infringement by defendant, and damages. Production of the patent or certified copy makes a prima facie case on patentability and validity and (if plaintiff is patentee) on title and may satisfy initial burden on inventive act; thereafter the burden shifts to the defendant to overcome presumptions of patentability, validity, and ownership by clear and satisfactory evidence removing every reasonable doubt. Where defendant files a special plea, burden rests on the party with the affirmative as finally closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's interpretation limits admissible evidence about invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent covers the invention(s) which the court, in construing its provisions, decides it describes and claims; evidence inconsistent with that construction is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties and jury must proceed on the court's construction; evidence offered under any other view is inadmissible and a verdict based on it is contrary to law. The court may use testimony, expert evidence, and Patent Office papers connected with the patent or known to the inventor at application date to explain terms or ascertain essential characteristics, but the interpretation must be based on the patent as it stands and cannot be limited or extended by extraneous evidence. Patents offered by defendant to defeat a plaintiff's patent cannot be made admissible by extraneous evidence. File-wrapper and contents are not admissible to limit the construction of the patent (file-wrapper cannot be used to narrow claim scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence as to the state of the art at the invention date
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of the state of the art at the date of conception is always admissible to show what was then known, to distinguish new features from old, and to define the limits of the inventive act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such evidence requires no prior notice and may be printed/written documents, witnesses familiar with the art, or specimens/exhibits. It can narrow the field of invention and limit inquiry. However, evidence applicable to defenses that require notice cannot be considered by the jury on such defenses unless the necessary notice was given. Earlier foreign provisional specifications or models may be admissible to show state of the art. State-of-the-art evidence cannot be used to 'anticipate' the invention unless that issue is properly pleaded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of evidence by estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence otherwise admissible may be excluded if the witness or party is estopped by prior record or conduct from asserting contrary facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party cannot deny the truth of documents or assertions by which he induced another to act. Examples: a patentee cannot assert patent is worthless or abandoned against his assignee; a disclaimer prevents claiming the disclaimed part was embraced in the invention; admissions in the application or specification estop patentee from denying validity; an assignor cannot testify against his assignee to defeat title. Estoppel rests on preventing a party from deceiving another by subsequent contradiction of induced beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence applicable to the defense that invention lacked inventive skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The question whether the alleged invention involved inventive skill is for the jury in view of the state of the art, unless lack of inventive skill is apparent on the patent's face, in which case the court may declare the patent invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden on plaintiff is satisfied by introducing the patent; defendant must overcome the prima facie presumption with evidence. Reduction to practice need only be shown by the specifications and drawings when the invention is thus adequately described. If the patent's description shows obviousness, the court may take judicial notice and rule invalid without submitting to jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of models, rejected applications, and foreign documents to show circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Models, rejected applications of third persons, and earlier foreign provisional specifications may be used to show the circumstances of the invention and the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such items are admissible in connection with evidence that the patentee knew of them to give construction to the patent. An earlier provisional specification (e.g., English) may show the state of the art and thus negative invention; models and rejected applications may narrow the field of invention and limit inquiry. However, these items cannot be used to vary or enlarge the claims by extraneous evidence.
